[[RunningHead]]

Freud and Said

Joseph Berke

Joseph Berke

London N6 5AG

Joseph Berke  

Dear Editor

I read with interest Marco Chiesa's review of Freud and the Non-European by Edward Said in the BJP (21(1): 153-5). Unfortunately the reviewer uncritically repeats the many errors of fact, and distortions, which occur in Said's writings.

If Said queried Freud's Jewish identity, one might well query Said's Palestinian identity. Recent information shows he was born, not in Palestine (as he claimed), but in Egypt of a well-to-do family which did subsequently move to Palestine, but later chose to move to the USA. However, the Internet has him born in Jerusalem, moving to Cairo at a very young age, and then to the States.

Said always claimed he was an objective academic. On the contrary he was a Palestinian nationalist and activist, and an unaffiliated member of the Palestinian National Congress. Perhaps the truth of his position was evident a couple of years before he died when he was filmed throwing rocks into Israel (with other Palestinian militants) at the Lebanese border.

Said inhabited an ‘Alice in Wonderland’ universe where victimizers became victims, and projective processes took the place of political activism, in particular, with regard to Arab and Palestinian aggression. Significantly, Said's work has itself been thoroughly discredited by the historical scholar, Ephraim Karsh (1999, 2000).

One cannot go over the whole history of Arab-Jewish relations in a short letter. It is worthwhile pointing out, however, that Arab extremists were setting off bombs in the heart of Jerusalem as far back as the 1920s and 1930s with devastating consequences.

For any readers who might like to follow the facts more closely, I recommend The Complete Idiot's Guide to Middle East Conflict by the political scientist, Mitchell Bard (1999).

As for Freud's Jewish identity, this is an area which I, and my colleague, the psychoanalyst Professor Stanley Schneider of the Hebrew University, Jerusalem, have studied in considerable detail. It is unfortunate to base an argument on one of Freud's last works, Moses and Monotheism, an extraordinary conjecture which Jewish scholarship demonstrates has no basis in fact (see Yerushalmi 1991).

Notes on Mentalizing - Old Hat, or New Wine?

Jeremy Holmes MD FRCPsych

Jeremy Holmes

[email: j.a.holmes@btinternet.com]

Jeremy Holmes  

The terms mentalization and mentalizing have recently emerged in the psychoanalytic and psychodynamic literature, especially in relation to the treatment of people suffering from borderline personality disorder. This paper discusses the meaning, phenomenology, and clinical applications of the concept. Mentalizing can be related to similar ideas developed in relation to autism under the heading of ‘theory of mind’; Bion's alpha function in relation to deficits in thinking in people with psychotic processes; and a body of francophone psychoanalytic literature related to people suffering from somatization disorders who have difficulty in finding a language to describe emotions. In focusing on failure of mentalizing in people with borderline personality disorder, Fonagy and his co-workers have put forward a developmental theory in which the ability to monitor one's own and others' thought processes is compromised. Clinical examples are described and the advent of this new concept into the psychoanalytic vernacular is welcomed.

Dennis Brown

Richard Carvalho

Richard Carvalho

Richard Carvalho  

Many readers of the BJP will have known Dennis Brown who was on the Editorial Advisory Panel of the Journal, and will have heard the very sad news of his death at the comparatively early age of 76. Various formal obituaries have already appeared, which leaves me free to write one that is a little more personal about a man who commanded very great affection and respect for reasons that I hope will become apparent.

Dennis was born, a twin, in 1928, and qualified in medicine at Leeds in 1951, ‘a triple bachelor’ as he put it, going on to become a Fulbright scholar at Cornell College in the United States. Here he became interested in dermatology, writing a dissertation on the psychological aspects of dermatitis. On his return to this country, he specialized in psychiatry, working as a lecturer at Leeds University. His decision to train as a psychoanalyst brought him to London where he worked as a medical assistant at the Cassel Hospital and as a research assistant to Sir Denis Hill at the Middlesex. His findings became the basis of what was to become his MD thesis, ‘A study of the significance of psychological symptoms in eczema’. He subsequently became consultant psychotherapist at St George's Hospital between 1969 and 1974, thereafter going as consultant psychotherapist to St Mary's Hospital in Paddington. Here he worked with his fellow consultant psychotherapist Jonathan Pedder with whom he wrote their justly acclaimed Introduction to Psychotherapy.

I was both honoured and fortunate to join him in 1980, when Jonathan had retired. We worked together in the therapeutic milieu which operated on all the wards and in the day hospital. Together, we were able to assess something over a hundred patients a year for individual and group psychotherapy, most of whom were seen under our supervision within the department of psychiatry until political and funding arrangements made this impossible.

Dennis retired in 1987, angry essentially, both at the divisions in the department and at the political situation in which it was hard to see anything constructive. But he was also very tired, and seemed to shed ten years overnight once he had left. He went on to concentrate on his work at the Group Analytic Practice, in the Institute of Group Analysis and with the European Association for Transcultural Group Analysis. In 1994, he published a book he had co-authored with the late Louis Zinkin on developments in group analytic theory, The Psyche and the Social World, as well as several papers on group analytic practice. His collected papers, ‘Resonance and Reciprocity’, are to be published shortly by Routledge.

[[RunningHead]]

Consciousness is Biological, Social and Individual

Anthony Ryle

Anthony Ryle

West Sussex [rylecat@aol.com]

Anthony Ryle  

Dear Editor

The papers in the Autumn 2004 number of the Journal (BJP 21(1)) concerned with the neglected topic of consciousness point to, but also manifest, many of the unresolved problems in this field. In this letter I would like to comment on some of them and then to propose an understanding which overcomes many of the obstacles.

In the first place it is important to reject the assertion that consciousness is not amenable to scientific understanding. Here, as often, William James has something to say. He observed that ‘All our thinking today has evolved gradually out of primitive thought, and the only really important changes have come over its manner … are a greater hesitancy in asserting its convictions, and a habit of seeking verification for them whenever it can’ (James 1911, pp. 15-16). He adds that:

the extraordinary progress of the last three hundred years is due to a rather sudden finding of the way in which a certain order of questions ought to be attacked, questions admitting of mathematical treatment. But to assume that the only possible philosophy must be mechanical and mathematical, and to disparage all enquiry into the other sorts of question, is to forget the extreme diversity of aspects under which reality undoubtedly exists. (pp. 23-4, my italics)

I would argue that only by adopting a far narrower definition of science than that offered by James could one justifiably exclude consciousness from scientific study. Consciousness is, of course, one of the ‘other sorts of question’, and ‘mechanical and mathematical methods’ have only a limited contribution to make. But before we resort to mystical or introspective approaches, there is a place for the accurate description of how consciousness is experienced and of how meanings may be expressed in the dispositions, activities and affects of people. And we can trace the history of these in the evolution of Homo sapiens and their development in individuals.

Consciousness is accompanied by brain activity but the mind-brain issue is not resolved by Colman (BJP 21(1): 83-102) when he quotes Papineau as saying that ‘brain function is experience and that's it’. Simply declaring that two sets of disparate phenomena which are functionally linked in complex ways are the same involves an elementary category mistake and can only spread confusion. Black (BJP 21(1): 69-82)

Response to Joseph Berke

Marco Chiesa

Marco Chiesa

London SW14 8JH [marco@cassel.ftech.co.uk]

Marco Chiesa  

Dear Editor

Joe Berke asserts that my review (BJP 21(1), pp. 153-5) ‘uncritically repeats the many errors of fact, and distortions, which occur in Said's writings’. However, Dr Berke does not bring any specific argument based on evidence sufficient to refute the points contained in the book reviewed.

To argue (from which source?) that Said was not born in Palestine, when it is universally recognized that he was born in Jerusalem, is puzzling. To criticize Said's arguments on the basis that they are rooted in ‘one of Freud's last works’, when (a) Moses and Monotheism is the most comprehensive contribution made by him on the subject and (b) it is widely recognized that some of Freud's most outstanding contributions are contained in his later work, is at the same time remarkable and dismissive.

To depict Freud's devotion to Judaism as a semi-clandestine activity (‘the covert Freud’ in Berke's own words) affected by the ‘prevalent anti-Semitism in Eastern Europe’ seems very hard to reconcile with a picture of a man who did not hesitate to challenge contemporary views on sexuality, who developed a revolutionary discipline, who was not afraid of the Gestapo and ridiculed it as he left Austria for London. Furthermore, to suggest that Freud's ambivalence to Judaism was opportunistically driven verges on the disrespectful.

A debate on these issues is welcome, but Dr Berke takes on the all too familiar position of disqualifying the work of two scholars like Said and Rose by personally attacking them, while presenting his own views and findings as objective. The tone and content of his letter show that he is far from being immune to bias on this subject.

Yours sincerely

The Specificity of Torture as Trauma: The Human Wilderness When Words Fail

Marcelo N. Viñar

The author attempts to situate the specificity of torture - understood as the product of political violence and of totalitarian states - within the historical framework of the concept of trauma in psychoanalysis. When the mind and social ties are simultaneously affected, the intrapsychic and transpersonal aspects of the suffered damage intertwine in a complex and unique web. The author aims to dismantle the notion of victim, considering it both stigmatizing and inaccurate. The goal is not just to identify the after-affects and the disabilities suffered by those affected by torture, but also to integrate their experiences and their narratives into a life project. Rather than individual psychopathology, this essay reflects upon those phenomena of suggestion and hypnosis that are at work in human groups under ordinary conditions and that are exacerbated under social crises, following the Freudian axis developed in Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego.



International Journal of Psychoanalysis86, 775-799, 2005

Why Perversion? ‘False Love’ and the Perverse Pact

Ruth Stein

In this paper, the author works with the awareness that perversion is a socially, historically and theologically loaded term, at the same time as it may be the latest frontier in psychoanalysis, both clinically and in relation to contemporary art and culture which emphasize the perverse. Positioning itself against tendencies to deny the existence of a category of ‘perversion’ or, inversely, to abuse it for the power that accrues from the act of diagnosing, she also points to other liabilities in the history of the treatment of this term, such as the narrowing down of perversion to the exclusively sexual domain, or, alternatively, the over-extension of it to polymorphously erotic practices that enhance sexual excitement. The paradoxes of perversion and the difficulties of distinguishing the perverse from the non-perverse are addressed. The case is also made that, in order to understand perversion, one must unlink it from the narrow notion of sexual practice and see what is involved on a deeper level - an approach initiated when psychoanalysis turned to perversion as a defence against psychotic anxieties, and began considering the necessary place of perversion in the transference-countertransference. Two features common to both sexual and non-sexual perverse relations are the seductive and bribing aspects of perversion, and its means-ends reversal. Perversion is a haven for the disguising of hatred and suspicion as excitement and (false) love. Displaced child and beating father, entitled child and seductive mother, are both prototypes of psychoanalytic reflection on parents who excite, deceive and corrupt their children and establish perverse pacts with them. The notion of the perverse pact is foregrounded in Alice's analysis, where first the resurrection and then the dismantling of such a pact were effected through various analytic means.

Christopher MacKenna

Christopher MacKenna

London

Christopher MacKenna  

The relationship between psychoanalysis (in a wide sense) and religion has passed through several stages. With Freud, there was outright opposition. Jung, on the other hand, believed that the religious ‘instinct’ is a natural function which, for many people caught in the post-religious twentieth century Western world, was better catered for in an analytic setting than by an attempted return to the patient's religious roots - though he did not exclude this possibility with those for whom it was still possible. Since 1961, when Jung died, the social and intellectual climate in this country has changed considerably, and analytic thinking has advanced in a number of ways which now enable us to be more thoughtful about the possibilities of religious experience. Josephine Klein's book, Jacob's Ladder (Klein 2003), is one fruit of this new learning, daring to wonder, as she does, whether religious experience may not contain treasures to which analytic thinking has yet to find access. Agneta Schreurs has made another significant contribution to this debate. Her book, Psychotherapy and Spirituality (Schreurs 2002)

Editorial

Karl Figlio

Karl Figlio

[kfiglio@essex.ac.uk]

Karl Figlio  

Men clothe themselves in masculinity; that is, they take on their character as apparel, and fear losing it just as easily as they put it on. That is the profound point of the old proverb and the title of Tom Ryan's paper, ‘Clothes maketh the man’.

In public life, cultural productions, including psychoanalysis, are among the clothes through which men become masculine. The masculinity of these cultural productions can also be as easily removed as they were put on. Almost as soon as Freud said in 1923 that the boy built his identity on an identification with father (p. 31), clinical attention turned to the complexities and vicissitudes of dis-identification with mother. In 1926, Karen Horney recast the inferiority and the penis envy of the female, the castrated male of classical psychoanalytic theory. She said, ‘The present analytical picture of feminine development differs in no case by a hair's breadth from the typical ideas that the boy has of the girl’ (p. 327). In other words, if a boy were a girl, he would feel inferior. By contrast, he clothes himself in his masculine superiority. From Horney on, the clothes of masculinity have been scrutinized in ever greater detail.

In this volume, Marie Maguire argues that there is a residual identification with mother, which is highly ambivalent. In cases in which father does not have, or is excluded from, a role in the boy's masculine identifications, these identifications may be based on mother's phallic potency and may remain insecure and conflicted. She explores the implications of these ambivalent identifications in the relationship between a female psychotherapist and a male patient.

Brian Denness elaborates on the ceremonies of initiation into manhood, which often involves physical marking of the body, such as tattooing or piercing, as the imposition of the reality of castration and of the paternal order. He argues that the paternal order can be radically avoided - preoedipally foreclosed, in Lacanian thinking - leaving the boy, concretely, without a masculine identity. His body modification then becomes a compulsive attempt to initiate himself into a paternal order.

Key Papers from the 1950s, IJPA Key Papers Series, edited by Andrew C. Furman and Steven T. Levy. Published by Karnac, London and New York, 2003; 306 pp; £19.99.

Victoria Davenport

Victoria Davenport

London

Victoria Davenport  

This is the fifth volume in the International Journal of Psychoanalysis Key Papers Series. Previously published books include The Mind-Brain Relationship, Psychoanalysis and Film, Key Papers on Countertransference and Key Papers on Borderline Disorders. Changing their slant slightly, the publishers have launched a sub-series in the form of decade-by-decade key papers, of which this - papers from the 1950s - is the first.

Why start with the 1950s? In their preface the joint chief editors of the IJPA explain that the 1950s, in their opinion, were a turning-point in the history of psychoanalytic thinking and practice, as the decade also was historically, politically and culturally. World War II caused many European psychoanalysts to emigrate to the United States, where their individual trainings and practices merged with American thinking of the time and, led to an impressive birth of creativity, in particular, to the concepts of egopsychology, of object relations, and to new thinking about the psychoanalytic relationship. In the editors' words, it was a period of the ‘turning of psychoanalytic attention from the exploration of the analysand's intrapsychic experience to mapping out equally relevant psychoanalytic concerns that exist outside the analysand's mind in connection with it’ (p. 1).

The well-known authors are all here, and there are few surprises in the editors' choice: Winnicott, Heimann, Little, Racker, Money-Kyrle, Bion, Segal, Balint, Bowlby, to name but a few.

Sexuality: A Biopsychosocial Approach by Chess Denman. Published by Palgrave Macmillan, Basingstoke, Hampshire, and New York, 2004; 368 pp; £17.99.

Celia Harding

Celia Harding

London

Celia Harding  

Dr Chess Denman, psychiatrist, Jungian analyst and cognitive analytical therapist, observes that, ‘sex remains a difficult subject to discuss with any sense of balance’ (p. 1). She offers a biopsychosocial approach to counteract the prejudices that she detects in existing approaches to sexuality, to inform therapists about sex and to encourage them to interrogate their unexamined assumptions. She provides composite clinical examples to illustrate her approach.

Denman explores sexuality from three angles. Beginning with a comprehensive and informative biological account she considers chromosomes, hormones, internal and external sex organs, brain differences, sexual response cycles, medical matters and evolutionary processes. Biology limits our sexuality: ‘Sex is a biological business. Large parts of what we do, how we wish to do it and how we have difficulty in doing it are strongly conditioned by biological factors’ (p. 36). The social/cultural dimension allows greater latitude for sexual variation: ‘It is the fact of sexual diversity across time, and across and within cultures, which undercuts easy claims of sexual universality and any easy standard of sexual normality’ (p. 37). Sexual health is gauged according to social standards, collective aims and values. At the psychological level individuals shape their personal sexuality from their socio-biological possibilities. Sexuality is ‘an intensely personal experience’, and scope for individual variation is greatest psychologically. She acknowledges psychoanalysis as the foremost contributor to the psychology of sexuality. She credits psychoanalysis with recognizing the importance of sexuality in human development and providing fertile soil for the erotic imagination. However, her even-handed and impressive coverage of the range of psychoanalytic theories is peppered by her negative evaluation of the social conservatism and prejudice she detects in privileging heterosexuality and monogamy and a tendency to ‘pathologize’ alternative sexualities despite accommodating polymorphous perversity and bisexuality within ‘healthy’ sexuality.

Michael Maconochie

London

Michael Maconochie  

Can the psychoanalytic and psychotherapeutic models be scaled up to work effectively at an institutional level? Does the process that works well in the consulting room between patient and therapist, or between group and

626

facilitator, translate into the language of business or other large enterprises like government or nationalized industry (health, education, transport and so on)? A lot of people hope it can be so. Their voices are heard particularly from the directions of academia, where social psychologists seek paid testing grounds for their theories; and from the consulting room too, where the sometimes lonely, sometimes underpaid practitioner may feel convinced that analytic insight and vision must surely apply on a broader stage.

Thus we have the analyst turned management consultant and, more recently, the therapist-cum-executive-coach or mentor. Related permutations have flourished around the world and nowhere has the ground proven more fertile than continental Europe. When the Continent's giant national corporate champions fall on hard times, simple capitalist remedies are seldom an option. They are too ‘Anglo-Saxon’ in philosophy, too Darwinian in tooth and claw. So some organizational therapy, couched in language of academic psychology, frequently finds a welcoming audience.

Two recent books by David Gutmann and Erik de Haan exemplify the tendency.

Professor Gutmann combines board membership of the International Association of Group Psychotherapy with the role of vice-president of the International Forum for Social Innovation. His book Psychoanalysis and Management: The Transformation is based on interviews with Oscar Iarussi, an Italian journalist, and is translated here from the French edition. A typical Gutmann patient/client was Bruno Lescoeur, of Electricité de France, but also from 1999 to 2002 chairman of its subsidiary, London Electricity Group. He contributes a glowing preface.

The Gutmann philosophy or spiritual standpoint or psychotherapeutic stance is necessarily eclectic: the product needs different packaging for different customers. His glossary is illuminating in this connection. Common terms become esoteric when placed in the service of ‘transformation’. Thus the central idea of progress by ‘zigzag’ is defined in terms of the contrast between Western and Chinese thought processes. References to ‘script’ are to be understood in the Eric Berne transactional analysis sense. And ‘transformation’ also carries meaning from rugby football. To convert a try in French is to transform it.

Bridging the Gap: Similarity and Difference between Psychoanalytic and Systemic Therapeutic Orientations

Mary Donovan

Mary Donovan

London N12 OJE. [email: mary.donovan@virgin.net]

Mary Donovan  

In recent times much has been made of integrative tendencies and common ground between therapeutic orientations, previously locked into highly oppositional frames. This is evident in the rapprochement between psychoanalysis and cognitive-behavioural therapy in adult mental health. It is a trend that is also evident in the shifting relationship between systemic and psychoanalytic orientations. This paper begins with an overview of factors influencing the wider integrative ethos before considering the specific circumstance of the relationship between systemic family therapy and psychoanalysis. The paper considers both the past history of oppositionality between the two orientations as well as some current developments that might facilitate a more creative dialogue. Particular attention is paid to issues of similarity and difference between the therapeutic relationship in systemic family therapy and the psychoanalytic framework of the transference/countertransference. Implications for therapeutic technique are explored. The aim is not to minimize difference but to encourage cross-fertilization between these therapeutic orientations in the interest of patients/families who may benefit from an integrated response.

A Clinical Conversation about Confidentiality

Lesley Murdin and Julian Stern

Julian Stern

St Marks Hospital, Harrow

Julian Stern  

LM: The clinical material raises many issues. It's difficult to know where to start. There seem to be many issues raised about notes and confidentiality about what sort of notes to write and what to do when asked for them.

JS: And so many levels too - the vignette refers not only to the therapist/patient interaction but also to his countertransference and, crucially in this case, to what he felt his supervisor was saying and his difficulty in internalizing that - so the conflict is not just between the therapist and patient but between the therapist and supervisor as well.

I found myself, when thinking about it, starting to jump into an ‘action frame of mind’ - should he or shouldn't he disclose the notes - and then realizing that part of the problem is the tendency to jump into action and not to consider all the different players. I suggest we leave the action to one side and think first about the principles.

LM: Yes, and the general principles do not always fit with the given situation, especially when there are so many things going on. There seems to be a question about who is still alive. The husband has died and the therapist is trying to find a way to ensure that he is not dead and the question is raised about how he will find a way to make sure he is not dead. Perhaps, through some reparation at this stage, and the therapist is trying to grapple with the issue about how he reinstates himself?

JS: Certainly when I was looking at the case there seemed to be multiple losses cropping up - the death of the husband, the loss of her country, the end of the relationship with the old people's home, the end of therapy and the therapeutic relationship and quite possibly the loss of the potential to have children. She had been married and her husband had died. How old was she - about 43? It was not made explicit but I imagine another loss was the impending or likely loss of her ability to be a mother to a child. The other thing I was thinking about was her sense of exclusion from so many dyadic relationships. She felt so excluded and pushed away by the relationship with the therapist, and by the man who complained and by the authorities at the old people's home. She finds an ally in the solicitor and puts the therapist in the position of being the excluded third party. He's getting a taste of what it is like to be excluded.

Editorial

Rachel Winter

Rachel Winter

[rachelwinterbjp@aol.com]

Rachel Winter  

In the last issue, we marked the 20th anniversary of the Journal by remembering how the BJP came into being, and why. Appropriately, questions of identity and origins, of giving and receiving and of loss and recollection are the themes that emerge in this issue.

Anthony Ryle opens by challenging the large claims made for the contribution to psychotherapy of Evolutionary Psychology, a theory that has been widely presented as a revolutionary new science, a way to bring together all the behavioural sciences within a Darwinian perspective.

Anthony Winston follows with a brief survey of theories about anorexia nervosa, followed by a case history of ‘Simon’, demonstrating how in anorexia the nutritive/toxic link to the mother is forcibly broken in a ‘no-entry’ defence against invasion by unwanted projections, with dire consequences for the development of identity.

Turning from the need to keep things out to the need for acceptance and exchange, Mark Evans discusses unconscious motivations for gift-giving in psychotherapy. He describes three incidents from a single therapy to illustrate how gift-giving as a process can change over time.

On 13 August 2004 Donald Meltzer, a major figure in our profession, died. Amongst the papers accepted for publication that I inherited from Ann Scott were one of his later ruminations on thought disorder - with characteristic relish he repeatedly refers to this in the words of an analysand, as ‘shit cream’ - and a companion paper by Meg Harris Williams, considering Bion's three ‘vertices of knowledge’, science, art and religion. These papers will be seen by some as provocative, by others as thought-provoking, original heuristic contributions.

Meg Harris Williams, in her obituary of Dr Meltzer in our last issue, told us that his nickname at school was Tubby Belcher, a reference to his size and pugnacity. He had strong views and inspired strong feelings. We publish here one of his last interviews, on the subject of supervision. He loved being interviewed, as he told Robert and Mirta Oelsner on this occasion.

Response to anthony Ryle

David Black

David Black

[dmblack@clara.co.uk]

David Black  

Dear Editor

Thank you for giving me a chance to respond to Dr Ryle's letter. At the beginning, he rejects the arguments of some of the contributors on consciousness in your recent issue (BJP 21(1), Autumn 2004). I'll comment on the points that relate to my own paper.

I presume I am one of the targets of Dr Ryle's first numbered paragraph

471

- I said I thought science as we have known it since Galileo (four centuries ago for us, three centuries ago for William James) cannot encompass the fact of consciousness. Dr Ryle appears to disagree. However, his quotations from James, with whom he then appears to agree, are precisely along the lines of my own argument, and the second one is virtually a summary of the point my paper was making. I think Dr Ryle has confused the issue by implying James is offering a definition of ‘science’. In fact, James is carefully using the word ‘philosophy’, presumably because he is acutely aware what a linguistic minefield these arguments tread in. (I am always happy to find myself in agreement with William James who, in his breadth of interest and determination to keep psychology in touch with philosophy, is very much one of my own sources of inspiration.)

In his second paragraph, Dr Ryle claims that to equate brain function with experience is a category mistake. I agree entirely. But he then says I provided a ‘supreme example’ of this mistake when I suggested that brain science may come to show us more precisely what we mean by some of the terms we derive from introspection. Here I think he has misunderstood my point. I illustrated it by using the example of memory. By introspection, we become aware that we seem to have different sorts of memory.

Neuroscience can help us to see clearly that there are indeed different sorts of memory - short-term, episodic, procedural, semantic, etc - by showing that they are stored in different locations in the brain. This clarifies the fact that they truly are different sorts of memory, not merely different versions of a single thing, and therefore confirms that we are right to use different terms to describe them. This argument doesn't ‘equate’ brain function with experience - a view I explicitly reject in my paper - but it does assume that brain functioning and experience correlate with one another, a view which I don't think Dr Ryle wishes to dispute.

Painting, Psychoanalysis, and Spirituality by Stephen James Newton. Published by Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 2001; 264 pp; £60.00.Psychological Aesthetics: Painting, Feeling and Making Sense by David Maclagan. Published by Jessica Kingsley, London and Philadelphia, 2001; 157 pp; £16.95.

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers

Canterbury

Janet Sayers  

These two books are highly illuminating. They reiterate, in terms of art and psychoanalysis, a major post-war revision of Freud's theory of unconscious primary process towards much greater recognition of its fluid interconnection with secondary process consciousness. Marion Milner attributed this revision, at least in part, to ‘problems raised by the nature of art’ (Milner 1956, p. 211). Winnicott attributed it to learning from analysing schizophrenics during World War II that our initial, primary state of mind is one of ‘unintegration’ of which he wrote:

There are long stretches of time in a normal infant's life in which a baby does not mind whether he is many bits or one whole being, or whether he lives in his mother's face or in his own body, provided that from time to time he comes together and feels something. (Winnicott 1945, p. 150)

Citing Winnicott approvingly, Klein characterized our first, primary process experience as, in a sense, bounded in consisting of object-related paranoid-schizoid anxieties and defences, these intermeshing with manic and depressive states of mind involving the integrating effect of experiencing others as loved, loving and good.

Psychoanalytic Dialogues14(4): 405-422, 2004

Race for Cover: Castrated Whiteness, Perverse Consequences

Gillian Straker

What happens when governments, institutions, or associations betray our most cherished values and ideals? Through the tropes of melancholia, perversion, and the fetish, this paper examines the complex reactions that such a betrayal may elicit.

The author argues that betrayal evokes shame and guilt by association, and that it also engenders the complicated form of mourning implicated in melancholia. A person may disavow the betrayal itself in order to deal with these painful reactions. This disavowal may then become stabilized via the use of the fetish in its various forms (e.g. the commodity fetish, the body fetish, and the fantasy fetish). This has perverse consequences, including subtle enactments of racism and other forms of marginalization and exclusion of Otherness.



Psychoanalytic Dialogues14(4): 503-515, 2004

Playing with the Reality of Analytic Love: Commentary on Paper by Jody Messler Davies ‘Falling in Love with Love’

Peter Fonagy and Mary Target

Responding to Davies's extension of the classical psychoanalytic description of the Oedipus complex, the authors argue that, in theoretical thinking about the Oedipus complex, attachment and sexual relating must be carefully distinguished, although they ceaselessly interact and - in the end - their separate contributions may be hard to disentangle. Making this distinction enables these authors to suggest that it is less likely to be a refusal of romantic response that triggers the patient's relentless pursuit of love from the analyst than an earlier disorganization of the infantile attachment. Taking the transference situation as a whole, the patient's persistent demand for an unattainable gratification can then be seen as the patient's determination to create in the consulting room another person who is in beleaguered, defensive withdrawal from a relationship. The discussion further elaborates the similarities and differences between the authors' own theoretical position and Davies's relational perspective through a consideration of the case of Roberta presented by Davies in her paper.

The BJP, standing as it does at the interface between BCP and UKCP, occupies a unique place in the landscape of the profession which it seeks to reflect, entertain and inform. After six months in the editorial eyrie, I've been considering the future direction of the BJP - what do I want, what does the Board want, what do readers of the Journal want? And what do we need? What can the Journal offer that might help our profession mature? Conceptual development, clinical adventures, defining and refining of theories, clear and creative thinking and … what else?

I should very much like to hear from anyone who has thoughts and suggestions about this because over the next months we shall be trying our wings and looking into various possibilities both at home and abroad. We are developing a section on ‘Addictive States of Mind’, for which we invite submissions and I hope to commission a regular Letter from America and perhaps an American issue. Next year will be the 150th anniversary of Freud's birth and 60 years since the first appearance of the paranoid-schizoid position in ‘Notes on some schizoid mechanisms’ (Klein 1946). We welcome papers and occasional pieces, including poems and artworks, on these or other 2006 anniversary themes. Our next issue will consider aspects of Masculinity under the paternal eye of guest editor Karl Figlio and from time to time we shall be inviting other guest editors to collaborate on special themed issues. If you have suggestions for themes, again, please write to me.

In this issue we present you with a delicious feast of papers, opening with Kenneth Wright's lyrical exposition of the poetic and therapeutic uses of language to convey living experience. Laurence Spurling gives an account of using combined individual and group therapy in work with borderline patients and Jane Polden revisits the drive to reparation and the forms it might take. Lord Alderdice applies psychoanalytic thinking to the origins of terrorism from his extensive experience of working in Northern Ireland. Jo Klein encourages us to open up the topic of spirituality for wider and lively discussion.

Josephine Klein  

Fish (fly-replete, in depth of June,

Dawdling away their wat'ry noon)

Ponder deep wisdom, dark or clear,

Each secret fishy hope or fear.

Fish say, they have their Stream and Pond;

But is there anything Beyond?

This life cannot be All, they swear,

For how unpleasant if it were!

One may not doubt that, somehow, Good

Shall come of Water and of Mud;

Wendy Gairdner  

The organization of this book into two volumes, entitled Exploring Feeding Difficulties in Children and Exploring Eating Disorders in Adolescents, under the overall title of The Generosity of Acceptance, has clearly been carefully considered. Anorexia nervosa and bulimia usually emerge in adolescence when the young person is grappling with the vicissitudes of sexual development and the pressure to begin to move away from the family into the outside world. But how, then, do we understand the self-starvation of pre-adolescent children? Can their problems also be seen as eating disorders? This book succeeds, partly by virtue of its separately titled volumes, in signalling the differences between these age groups whilst, at the same time, suggesting that there are many common issues connecting the cases of children and adolescents. In particular, the fear of dependence and of accepting from another and the associated strategies of defence are recurrent themes in the case studies of both volumes and provide the overall title of the book. This title also refers to the need for generosity in clinicians who must accept the sometimes violent projections of their patients.

Both volumes consist of collections of case discussions written by current and past members of the Eating Disorders Workshop in the Adolescent Department of the Tavistock Clinic and by clinicians in Italy who have completed Tavistock-model courses in child and adolescent psychotherapy. The introduction, which is common to both volumes, outlines the main themes of the book and provides a useful overview of the psychoanalytic thinking, based on Klein's theory of object relations, underpinning the case discussions. It outlines two main themes: the failure in some aspects of the early dyadic relationship between mother and infant, and the failure to work through the oedipal situation. Drawing on Bion's notion of the mother-infant relationship as container-contained (Bion 1962), it is suggested that there has been a reversal of this relationship so that the infant is not only not adequately contained but also becomes the receptacle of parental projections. For some, the editors suggest, the introjection of projecting objects can become unbearable and there is a need to disgorge, emit or block off these ‘missiles’. This may result in the development of a system of ‘no-entry defences’ (Williams 1997) in which there is an attempt to prevent the taking of anything into body or mind.

Journal of Analytical Psychology49, 521-551, 2004

Identity, Narcissism and the Emotional Core

Marcus West

This paper describes the course of an analysis which demonstrates how borderline and narcissistic functioning can be understood in terms of a struggle with issues of identity. It shows how such functioning can come to exert a profound hold on the individual and why it seems, at times, a matter of life and death to the patient to avoid states of separation from the analyst. The paper suggests that these complex phenomena can be understood, perhaps surprisingly, in the simple terms of the nature of affect itself. The concept of the emotional core is introduced to embody and highlight that which lies beneath both Jungian and Freudian models (offering a potential bridge between the two models) - namely the psyche's essentially affective nature. It is suggested that the emotional core can serve as an organ of perception giving the individual both their primary relation to reality and an emotional attachment to others. This emotional core is understood to function in a narcissistic manner to preference experiences of sameness and in aversion to experiences of difference - a view consonant with Stern's understanding of infant development where the infant is able to distinguish self from other from the beginning of life (as Fordham also held); taking up Stern's terminology, it gives the individual a ‘core’ sense of being. There is, however, no stable, ongoing sense of ‘I’ associated with this form of functioning as the individual is immersed in the latest affect to enter consciousness (as in the borderline state of mind), and consequently the individual comes to rely intensely on the other to determine their sense of being (the other becomes a self-regulating other in Stern's terms). The development of ego-functioning gives a more stable and ongoing sense of ‘I’ to the individual, giving contact with the broader personality, allowing the individual to be less reliant on the other and orientating them to reality in a way more fitting to their overall needs.

Christina Wieland  

This is the third volume by the Committee on Women and Psychoanalysis (COWAP) which has been set up to explore sexuality, interactions, and relationships between men and women. It is quite an ambitious book in its scope and breadth, but at the same time quite uneven. It is not only a mixture of different approaches and styles, but also a mixture of different levels of discourse, so that to talk about it as a unified whole is difficult. In the Introduction Alcira Mariam Alizade writes:

This book is intended to be open-minded and free-ranging in spirit…. The contributors were selected on a basis that combined both chance and known professional skill, with the idea of theoretical pluralism uppermost in our minds, even though we realized that this would probably result in controversy. (Foreword, p. vii)

I think that it is not the theoretical pluralism or the controversy that is the problem, but exactly the different levels of discourse ranging from the professional, theoretical or clinical, psychoanalytic approach to the more polemical or simply journalistic one.

The book is mainly, but not exclusively, the product of North and South American writers, and seems to have a double agenda of an in-depth exploration on the one hand, and promoting political/social change in male-female relations on the other. It comprises 11 articles, some psychoanalytic, some psycho-socio-political, some social psychological and not all worth reading. Some articles attempt to tackle topical themes such as transsexual surgery and its psychological causes and consequences, the involvement of men in abortion, male impotence and men's current insecurity of identity, but often the treatment of these themes is sketchy and full of generalizations. On the whole I found the book quite uneven with some papers much more light-weight than others. There is no new material in terms of theories of masculine development but maybe what is new is that masculinity and its vicissitudes are viewed from so many different angles. The book is informative and a good read for those who want an introduction to the subject.

Marion Gow  

This book was originally published in 1995, under the same title as above. Marie Maguire has written a completely revised edition in 2004 updating her critique on masculinity and femininity asserting that cultural idealization of men remains intact and that this is replicated in psychoanalytic theory and practice. The topics covered in the book focus on a contemporary psychoanalytic take on male and female power relations and sexuality, and this version includes more material on areas under-represented in psychoanalysis, e.g. racism in psychoanalytic theory, where she uses material from a number of sources, including the paper by US academic Jean Walton (1995) ‘Replacing race in [white] psychoanalytic discourse: founding narratives of feminism’ where she is critical of Joan Riviere's classic paper on ‘Womanliness as a masquerade’ (Riviere 1929). Walton argues that ‘throughout the decades psychoanalysts have consistently used white European subjectivity to represent all female identity’ (Maguire, p. 34), and further that Riviere does not comment at all on her patients' racialized fantasies. Importantly, Maguire explores the territory of racialization and racism in psychoanalysis, just as she continues to examine sexual power relations between men and women giving some very useful clinical material to demonstrate her case psychotherapeutically. Class, the Cinderella subject of psychoanalysis, is also given more space in this revised version inquiring into racist, sexist and classist methods of thinking between men and women and in psychoanalysis. In Chapter 4 she updates and presents clinical material to demonstrate the relevance of combining those issues with interrogation of power relations and how they are ‘structured into the male psyche’ (p. 12).

Dodi Goldman

Dodi Goldman

New York

Dodi Goldman  

We are all worms. But I do believe I am a glow-worm. (Winston Churchill)

Within the psychoanalytic movement, Masud Khan's reputation hovers somewhere between inspiration, curiosity and blight. Khan, after all, made intriguing theoretical contributions, helped some patients, provided valuable editorial assistance to prominent analysts, inflicted irreparable damage on people who deserved better, and wreaked serious havoc on the integrity of his profession. He could be brutally honest and maddeningly mendacious. He vigorously fabricated for the sake of posterity and disdained those who, he said, ‘have lost the verve of imaginative truth through escaping into tape-recorder-clinical realism’. When the idea of removing Khan from membership in the British Psycho-Analytical Society was first entertained, Anna Freud remarked: ‘If we do not throw him out, we have further trouble ahead - whereas if we do, we deprive ourselves of one of our most gifted people.’

Roger Willoughby, in his biography of Khan, places his faith in the adjudicating power of facts to make sense of all this. For Willoughby, historical evidence serves a ‘paternal function dissolving narcissistic and symbiotic illusions’. He tells us that he seeks to ‘move beyond the preferred myths to trace, via a psychoanalytic textual archaeology, the sometimes tellingly banal, but often more complex and intriguing realities of Khan's biography and intellectual history’. Willoughby hopes that by assembling facts he can illuminate Khan's dissembling.

Part of Willoughby's method is straightforward enough. He has combed the records of the British Society, interviewed numerous people who had dealings and relationships with Khan, perused exchanges of letters between colleagues and friends, and drawn heavily upon Khan's own work-books.

Editorial

Rachel Winter

Rachel Winter

[rachelwinterbjp@aol.com]

Rachel Winter  

Sometimes we compile articles for an issue with a particular subject in mind, such as the Special Issue on Masculinity. But often papers come together without a clear linking theme and it is interesting to try to see in what direction these bright threads might be leading us or what landscape these illuminations of thought might reveal.

We open this issue with a stimulating paper by Bob Hinshelwood considering how our individual and social identities depend on unconscious beliefs about what is inside us. He describes in detail an example of ‘chains of projection’, a process in which an individual emotional state travels through a group and, in so doing, changes from the personal to the institutional. He concludes that, ‘our internal world (identity) and our external world (reality) are under constant reconstruction and change’.

2005 brought the centenary of the publication of Freud's Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality of which Freud said, ‘Its insistence on the importance of sexuality in all human achievements and the attempt that it makes at enlarging the concept of sexuality has from the first provided the strongest motives for the resistance against psycho-analysis’ (Introduction to 1920 edition). In ‘The Inherent Shame of Sexuality’, Phil Mollon opens his paper by quoting from a sufferer from Tourette's Syndrome and then asks, ‘Why is such speech disturbing, embarrassing - shameful?’ He argues that language and culture are the product of displaced sexuality, the fig-leaves of the symbolic. Society develops from the discourse of shame.

The BJP/Freud Museum conference on 25 March 2006 will be the first in a series under the generic title, ‘Emerging Paradigms in Psychoanalysis’. The conference is entitled, ‘Mentalization: Who Thinks What?’ and will bring together practitioners from different theoretical backgrounds to consider the concept of mentalization in relation to other psychoanalytic models of mental functioning. We shall be publishing the conference papers and an account of the panel discussion in due course. Meanwhile, in this issue we open the debate with a lively paper by Jeremy Holmes entitled ‘Mentalization: Old Hat, or New Wine?’ in which he gives an account of the concept, its origins and clinical application in a clear, accessible way.

‘And What Rough Beast …?’: Psychoanalytic Thoughts on Evil States of Mind

Gavin Ivey PHD

Gavin Ivey

Private Bag 3, Wits 2050, Johannesburg, South Africa. [email: Iveyg@umthombo.wits.ac.za]

Gavin Ivey  

Evil is a concept traditionally alien to psychoanalytic discourse. Using a Kleinian framework it is argued that the term ‘evil states of mind’ usefully describes the experience of possession by a destructive personality suborganization founded on identification with a bad internal object. These states may be temporary and give rise to guilt and concern. In some cases, however, benevolent parts of the self are attacked and obliterated. The resulting loss is not experienced and mourned; instead perverse logic transforms it into a triumph. In this way the pain of loss and envy of the good possessed by others is denied, and psychic truth is replaced by perverse thinking in which good and bad are reversed. Satanic cults represent the pure organizational embodiment of the destructive subpersonality. Variants of evil states of mind are described with reference to psychotherapy patients and interviews with satanic cult members.

Marie Maguire

Marie Maguire

6 Stockwell Park Road, London SW9 0AJ. [email: mariemaguire2000@aol.com]

Marie Maguire  

I explore a bisexual male patient's need to differentiate highly problematic ‘feminine’ identifications - originating in childhood sexual abuse and impingement by men as well as women - from identifications with more admired aspects of his mother. My main focus is on the patient's sexual identity - the personal meaning he gave to being male - rather than on his bisexuality - his desire for both sexes. In psychoanalytic literature powerful opposite-sex identifications are usually associated either with psychotic confusion or celebrated as a source of psychic strength. The co-existence of problematic and highly valued cross-sex identifications is rarely discussed. I also look at how this patient re-negotiated his identity through the transference relationship with a female psychotherapist, given that his ‘masculinity’ derived mainly from childhood experiences of ‘stealing’ his mother's phallic power. Through a wide-ranging theoretical review I conclude that we need to draw together opposing psychoanalytic perspectives about maternal and paternal power, opening up new ways of thinking about triangular relationships in the transference.

This book represents a record of the supervision work carried out between Donald Meltzer and a group of psychoanalysts from Barcelona: Rosa Castellá, Lluis Farré and Carlos Tabbia. It was brought together as a tribute to Donald Meltzer and his work and is, quite literally, a publication of the transcripts of the original supervision sessions that were carried out between 1993 and 1998.

Following information about the contributors and the supervision arrangements the book is arranged in date order of supervision sessions. There are 22 supervision sessions overall, 15 of which are presentations of different patients with differing pathologies and the remaining seven are presentations of one patient, Eduardo. Each chapter is a supervision session and is named in relation to the patient and the particular piece of pathology on which the supervision session focuses. At the end of the book there are three different indexes which direct the reader to the central ideas, main subjects, and diagnoses covered by the book. The headings of the chapters and the three indexes help to orientate the reader in relation to the many themes that the book tackles within the framework of the supervision narratives.

The book starts with a chapter on the work of Lluis Farré with a patient called Lucía. This chapter reflects the format of the book in that it is a transcription of the analyst's presentation of the patient material, the session content and Meltzer's comments. As with all the chapters Meltzer's ideas and theories come alive via the presentation, by Lluis Farré, of Lucía. Meltzer elaborates on the patient's material and examines how Lucía exists within the claustrum, a claustrophobic world in which she is trapped in a battle between ‘submission or rebellion’ (p. 9). Meltzer also explores with Lluis Farré the more technical side of the work with this patient and how the language of interpretation does not engage her. Instead Meltzer advocates the language of journalism in which, through a technique more akin to an interviewer seeking information, the analyst can engage the patient in a ‘conversation’ so that ‘both you and she can understand what the fight is about’ (p. 13).

Nathan Field

London

Nathan Field  

The beneficial effect of disclosing our private thoughts and feelings, either to a confidant, priest, counsellor or therapist, has been acknowledged for centuries. Confession, as we all know, is good for the soul. More intriguing

251

is the fact that putting such thoughts into writing can be of equal benefit. Writers have long been aware that getting our persecutory ruminations out of our heads and down on to the page actually reduces their power over us. I have no doubt that keeping a private journal most of my adult life has helped me stay more sane and healthy than I might otherwise have been. So I find it puzzling that it has taken so long for analytical psychotherapy, so fertile in its production of analytic literature, to recognize writing as a valuable therapeutic agent in its own right?

This situation could begin to change with the publication of Writing Cures. To someone like myself, trained in the hothouse of analytical psychotherapy, the range of therapeutic writing techniques employed by the contributors to this handbook came like a breath of fresh air. They include the practice of narrative writing, described by Jane Speedy in Chapter 3 as a way of making sense of our personal lives in the context of our family history and social environment - and observing how it changes with emotional development. Another method is the use of letter writing in all its permutations: mainly letters to significant others, letters which will never be sent but manage to say what has never been said; or letters to oneself (perhaps the child one used to be, or the self one could possibly become?) or even letters to - and from - malfunctioning organs in one's own body. This approach is fascinatingly described in Chapter 8 by Stephanie Howlett in her work with patients suffering from chronic psychosomatic disorders, most of whom are seriously out of touch with their emotions and notoriously difficult to reach. Howlett, in quoting Joyce McDougall on ‘the discovery that certain people just have no words to describe their emotional states’, observes that writing can play a key role to overcome this condition, ‘… limited only by the imagination of the therapist’. Another important tool is journal writing, vividly described by Kate Thompson in Chapter 7. Its vital role over many years in cognitive-analytic therapy is described with admirable clarity by Anthony Ryle in Chapters 6 and 18.

Laurence Spurling

Laurence Spurling

Malet Street, London WC1E 7HX

Laurence Spurling  

This paper is an account of a programme of combined individual and group psychotherapy offered to borderline patients in an NHS setting. It is written from the perspective of an individual therapist and describes how he came to think of this therapy structure, which offers the patient two different therapy settings and a relationship with two different therapists, as a representation of the patient's entry into and negotiation of the Oedipus situation. The way each patient accommodates to this oedipal structure can be tracked by the therapists, and used in their thinking about and work with each patient. A case illustration is given of how one patient in the programme responded to the provision of two therapy modalities by massively and violently splitting her experience, denigrating and attacking one modality while appearing to value the other. The patient made no real progress until this splitting could be contained by the therapists. This allowed the patient to discover that there could be a generative link between the two settings. It is argued that it was this experience which played a crucial part in enabling the patient by the end of the programme to derive some benefit from the therapy as a whole.

Clothes Maketh the Man: Transvestism, Masculinity and Homosexuality

Thomas Ryan

Thomas Ryan

11 Cecile Park, London N8 9AX. [email: thomasjryan@blueyonder.co.uk]

Thomas Ryan  

The term transvestism is mistakenly applied to describe all categories of cross-dressing. This leads to theoretical and clinical confusion, as men who cross dress share some common features but differ greatly in regards to their aims and intentions. The aim of this paper is to provide an understanding of the formation and development of transvestism that extends beyond the classical psychoanalytic explanation of castration anxiety. Today, more emphasis is placed on anxieties emanating from the early symbiotic relationship with the mother, the formation of the sense of self and unresolved separation anxiety. Insights gained from clinical work with transvestites can enhance our understanding of the construction of masculinity and the male's greater gender conflicts and sexual insecurities. Also, the study of the homosexual fantasies or intense homophobia experienced by some fetishistic cross-dressers relate more to gender issues and conflicts than sexual orientation.

In Divine Therapy, subtitled Love, Mysticism and Psychoanalysis, Janet Sayers aims to bring to our attention the central place of love in the process of psychotherapy. She organizes our attention around two focal points: what she sees as the role of love in the lives of some well-known psychoanalysts, psychotherapists and related personages, and what she sees as the role of love in their theories of what goes on between therapist and patient.

Discussing love is undeniably a formidable task, in some ways made more difficult by the preconceptions we psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapists bring to the discussion. It is therefore practical for Janet Sayers to look at a number of eminent people operating in this field, with a special interest in the place of love in their lives: William James, Sigmund Freud, Carl Jung, Melanie Klein, Marion Milner, Erich Fromm, Paul Tillich, Wilfred Bion, Simone Weil, Donald Winnicott, Viktor Frankl, Julia Kristeva. I found the biographical information about each of them very interesting, and it will induce me to look at them in more detail and depth soon.

Brian Denness  

Prompted by the surprising reaction of a young man with a borderline personality to an interpretation of castration anxiety, this paper sets out to explore some of the unconscious determinants of tattooing and piercing. Recognizing that such acts can have an initiatory function, sociological, anthropological and psychoanalytic views of initiation and the role of the father in masculine development are examined. In some boys oedipal development is forestalled and castration anxiety is not experienced. A bifocal approach using object relations theories based on regression and Lacanian perspectives that highlight reactions to an oedipal impasse is used to understand these processes. Symbolic body modifications are differentiated from those that are non-symbolic.

Attachment in the Later Years: A Commentary

Phillip R. Shaver and Mario Mikulincer

We are grateful to Carol Magai and Nathan Consedine for inviting us to comment on the innovative articles in this special issue of Attachment & Human Development, which deals with attachment in late life. Attachment theory has gradually been extended from its original focus on affectional bonds between infants and their parental caregivers (e.g. Ainsworth, Blehar, Waters & Wall 1978; Bowlby 1969/1982) to adult romantic and marital relationships (e.g. Hazan & Shaver 1987; Mikulincer & Shaver 2003; Rholes & Simpson 2004) and now to older adults' close, sustaining relationships. The new focus falls within the intended scope of the theory; both Bowlby (1969/1982) and Ainsworth (1991) wrote theoretically about attachment across the lifespan. Until recently, however, there were few empirical studies of attachment in the later years, a phase of life that raises interesting questions about the reversal of roles between older adults and their grown-up offspring, the gradual reduction in number of relationship partners as a person ages, and the possible shift of caregiving functions from human relationship partners to God, other religious figures, and internalized images of lost partners (e.g. deceased parents, siblings, and spouses). These engaging topics are addressed in this special issue.



Psychoanalytic Dialogues15(1), 1-16, 2005

Revenge and Forgiveness in Laramie, Wyoming

Stephen Wangh

This author posits that, perhaps because of its religious implications, psychoanalysis has historically avoided speaking of forgiveness, although playwrights have often depicted forgiveness as a psychological mechanism that can help resolve cycles of anger and revenge. The Laramie Project (Kaufman et al. 2001), a play about how a US town deals with a murder and its aftermath, provides an example of the way in which forgiveness offers an exit from vengeance. The play points to both the positive and the negative roles that religious ideas play in human actions. At the same time, however, the play itself avoids some of the painful processes that enable human beings to locate forgiveness. This paper draws on psychoanalytic literature, social commentary, and plays by Aeschylus and Shakespeare to demonstrate how the mechanisms of forgiveness operate. In conclusion, it suggests that, although enabling the psychological processes of forgiveness can be extremely difficult, ignoring these processes may be life-threatening.

Clinical Commentary XXXIV

Sue Robinson and Jan Lee

Jan Lee

Jan Lee  

The situation of clinicians facing legal or procedural challenges is under researched in psychotherapy. Initial studies suggest that strong responses are engendered and that no matter how subtle or complex the material may have appeared in the consulting room, once it is the subject of legal process or institutional inquiry it rapidly becomes very concrete. Within organizations there is often acting out, even when there is not an actual complaint on the table. Those in the know may feel they stand as mute witnesses. In a fragmented profession like psychotherapy, it is not surprising that the scant existing research suggests that the personal experience of trying to understand and handle such issues can be a profoundly isolating one.

For these reasons dialogue has been placed at the heart of this commentary. Some time ago the joint editors, Sue Robinson and Jan Lee, began talking about the increasing threat posed to psychotherapy by litigation and complaints about practice and confidentiality. We asked two colleagues to hold a conversation on the subject of the exposure of clinical notes, as a way of furthering the discussion. Lesley Murdin (LM) and Julian Stern (JS) were selected because both have an interest in, and have published in the area of confidentiality and professional ethics. The dialogue theme was also reflected in the collaboration and conversations between the joint editors during the process of transcribing the conversation and preparing it for publication.

The rationale for this conversational format was also driven by the exigencies of the subject matter. In an area which is emergent and poorly understood, the illusion of relative certainty and closure fostered by authored comments seemed inappropriate. We saw value in using a conversation, in putting clinicians on the spot, as in professional practice and as in life. Hopefully, showing practitioners exploring uncertainty around questions that are potentially difficult and painful, and enabling readers to follow that process of exploration, will open up the debate. The reader is placed in a position of uncertainty and lack of clarity, similar to that held by clinicians trying to hold conversations in their consulting rooms. The discussion begins with a caution against action, proceeds to consideration of the supervisory relationship, before thinking about the role of shame and how to deal with the clinical problems raised when notes are requested for litigation purposes.

James Davies  

Frank Furedi's latest book is a provocative critique of ‘therapeutic culture’ and its impact on modern society. From its outset we are introduced to the controversial claim that ‘therapeutic culture [rather than strengthening individuals] has helped construct a diminished sense of self that characteristically suffers from an emotional deficit and possesses a permanent consciousness of vulnerability’ (p. 22). Furedi is certain that this ‘inner vulnerability’ is not entirely inherent to the human condition, but that it is rather in part ‘therapeutically constructed’, a construct which diminishes individuals in so far as it renders them fearful of their susceptibility to emotional damage. Thus, in an ironic reversal of what most therapists believe, Furedi holds that therapeutic practice, rather than alleviating social and individual ills, is contributing to the weakening of self and society.

Furedi reaches these conclusions by studying therapy as a cultural phenomenon, rather than as a clinical technique, a phenomenon that has served to redefine many experiences that have ‘hitherto been interpreted as part of life’ as damaging to peoples' emotional and psychological stability.

This clearly written book forms part of a series intended for those wishing to find out more about a career in mental health. It is concerned with psychoanalysis and provides a useful, basic introduction for anyone with an interest, but little prior knowledge of the field. It is divided into four main areas covering basic concepts, historical and cultural developments, the principal critiques of the discipline and the research base. With one caveat that I shall mention later, it succeeds admirably in de-mystifying and rendering accessible the theory and practice of psychoanalysis.

The first part of the book addresses the question of definition, and conveys the experience of the analyst and analysand, integrating this with an explanation of clinical concepts. The use of vivid, detailed clinical illustrations illuminates these concepts and elucidates what can seem to those unfamiliar with the psychoanalytic discourse as arcane, inaccessible ideas. The writing is particularly successful in conveying the clinical reality of the experience and the relevance of the concepts. It clarifies, in a down to earth way, how psychoanalysts use the theory to inform their practice.

John Alderdice

John Alderdice

Woodstock Lodge, 1 Woodstock Link, Belfast BT6 8DD, United Kingdom
email: alderdicej@parliament.uk

John Alderdice  

Descriptions of the phenomenon of terrorism have tended to concentrate solely on the external world and to polarize between socioeconomic explanations and the fight between good and evil. This paper takes a psychoanalytically informed approach to issues of causation and process. It explores the importance of meaning and history, regression and dissolution, and changes in the manifestations of communal violence over time. It sets out key features of the triangular tactic of what we generally understand as ‘terrorism’, but most significantly identifies the lasting power of feelings and the particular capacity of humiliation to generate violence.

The Shaping of Experience

Kenneth Wright

Kenneth Wright

6 Queen Street, Hadleigh, Ipswich, Suffolk IP7 5DZ. email: kjt.wright@doctors.org.uk

Kenneth Wright  

This paper explores how we sometimes manage, and often fail, to communicate the ‘feel’ of live experience. Since poetry makes a craft and vocation of this pursuit, the writings of poets are brought to bear on the process. I introduce the idea of containing forms, using the term containment in its everyday sense. My argument, however, owes much to Winnicott, Stern and Bion, Winnicott's transitional object exemplifying an early containing structure, and Stern's ‘attunement’ suggesting ways that later containing structures might arise out of mother-infant dialogue. Bion's more specific notions of containment and transformation are not explored. Following Langer, I suggest that feeling is better communicated through presentational rather than discursive symbols, such forms being concrete, sensory, and isomorphic in some way to that which is being shared. With such presentational symbols, resonance and dialogue between forms are more important than explanatory meaning and some implications of this for therapeutic discourse are discussed.

Gertrud Mander

Gertrud Mander

24 Chalcot Crescent, London NW1 8YD. [email: g.mander@virgin.net]

Gertrud Mander  

Resistance is encountered in psychotherapy in many different forms and can be seen as a survival strategy. This paper interprets the short story Bartleby the Scrivener by Herman Melville as a fictional case of defiant resistance which some patients develop to fend off external demands experienced as intolerable impingements. Clinical material from two particularly intractable cases of narcissistic damage is introduced in the second part of the paper to support the hypothesis that the therapist needs to contain and understand this kind of resistance as a defensive stance in the service of protecting a weak self structure, thereby making the patient feel held and enabled to shed the fear of impingement and to bear what Melville called the ‘cosmic orphanhood’ of man.

My Donald Meltzer

Stephen Wilson

Stephen Wilson

Campbell House, Campbell Square, Northampton NN1 3EB. [email: Stephen. Wilson@merton.oxford.ac.uk]

Stephen Wilson  

I began my analysis with Donald Meltzer about 30 years ago; I knew nothing about him and had been referred by Oliver Lyth, who had a more long-established local psychoanalytic practice. The choice was serendipitous, but the enduring course of my analysis was not. His consulting room was located upstairs in a small Victorian house, near the station, in a distinctly unsmart area of West Oxford. He and his wife, Martha Harris, who worked from a room at the front, shuttled between London and Oxford in an old Volvo Coupé, of which he was fond. At that time he lived in the Oxfordshire village of Brill. Among other things, he liked forestry, paintings, horses and Herman Melville. His couch was made from a piece of board, with a comfortable enough mattress on top, and he sat in a worn armchair, which I later discovered had belonged to his own analyst - Melanie Klein. His soft American accent had a kind of song-like quality, his voice seemed to hold and comfort, even as the content of what he said was starkly challenging. I soon began to appreciate the strength of his psychoanalytic conviction and uncompromising intellectual honesty.

Early on I dreamt that the consultant I was working with at Littlemore Hospital, Bertram Mandelbrote, had told me to go into his office and open up a parcel, as there was something inside for me. It turned out to be a gold and diamond encrusted watch with a lid that covered the dial. Apparently it had been given to Bertram by an American Drug Company. In the dream, my friend and colleague, Peter Agulnik (who had encouraged me to go into analysis), said, ‘It's bound to be good if that's where it comes from’. Clearly my enthusiasm for psychoanalysis, conveyed to me through Donald Meltzer, knew no bounds, yet it is interesting to note that the dial of the watch was covered up. It is as if the information, the knowledge conveyed by the watch-face, was obscured by a layer of idealization. Perhaps it is no coincidence

Anne Power

Anne Power

London

Anne Power  

This book presents six papers by members of the London Centre for Psychotherapy which the introduction suggests ‘show working psychotherapists trying to learn from their patients and from themselves’. The prospect of reading how colleagues struggle with and reflect on their work is always intriguing, and this collection succeeded in making me think about my own clinical work and about some of the dividing lines which run between different clinical styles and values.

Vivienne Lewin's chapter provides a useful account of some of the dynamics which may occur when working with a twin and she includes substantial outlines of a few cases. Her reflections on the twin in the transference make her work relevant to therapists who are not actually working with twins and she draws on Klein and Bion to explore the phenomenon of an imaginary twin. There are some interesting references to patients whose main defence is the avoidance of difference, and she quoted the fascinating example of a patient who left when Lewin could not see her at the time identical to that at which her twin was having a session with another therapist. I felt it could have been fruitful to explore this symbiotic relationship in terms of Mahler's theory of separation/individuation. The issues raised by Lewin are also explored in a paper by Anni Bergman (1971) who uses Mahler's theory to develop an exceptionally empathic relationship with a child who insisted on sameness with her mother. Bergman names the dilemma of the child who feels compelled to protect herself against difference: ‘I talked about how difficult it was for her to have me help her, because if I did help her, instead of magically making things turn out right, we became “I” and “you”, which made her afraid of being alone’ (p. 338). I sensed that there is a key difference between how Bergman and Lewin explore this issue with their patients, and that this difference is central to how each of us works.

I found Prophecy Coles's writing coherent and pleasurable to read; she conveys important ideas in a thoroughly accessible form. Her chapter on sibling attachment is one of those which lives up to the promise on the book cover about authors who ‘gradually find their way beyond the maps provided by their training and reading’. Her reflections on sibling transference are very useful and her observation that this transference ‘can arouse particular anxiety in both patient and therapist’ (p. 27) made sense of my own experience with patients. I felt also encouraged by her openness about her own work: she tells us that she found herself ‘much more vulnerable to a countertransference enactment when the sibling transference was predominant’ (p. 37).

Who Owns Psychoanalysis? edited by A. Casement. Published by Karnac, London, 2004; 396 pp; £19.99.

David Black

David Black

London

David Black  

The word psychoanalysis is used to mean two things that would be better given separate names. One is a large and ramifying body of theory about human emotional development, including its pathology; the other is a small group of rather similar sorts of psychotherapy. It is as if we used only one word to mean both botany and gardening.

The question posed by the title, ‘Who owns psychoanalysis?’, is therefore confusing and perhaps, strictly speaking, unintelligible. I think it has been carefully crafted, however, as a compendious way of suggesting a whole spectrum of similar-sounding but more specific questions. These include: who has the right to decide what constitutes a contribution to psychoanalytic theory? who can say a given technical innovation is or is not compatible with psychoanalytic practice? what organizations are entitled to train prospective psychoanalysts? and (that current hot potato on the British scene) who is entitled to call himself or herself a psychoanalyst?

In this large book (20 contributors, 18 chapters), Casement has assembled a wide range of views and personalities. They include such senior figures as the psychiatrist Thomas Szasz (who contributes with his customary clarity and vigour), the historian of psychoanalysis Paul Roazen, and the anti-Freudian philosopher Adolf Grünbaum. They include the Lacanian analysts Bernard Burgoyne, Darian Leader, Elizabeth Roudinesco and Dany Nobus, the historian Sonu Shamdasani, the philosophers Frank Cioffi and Jerome Wakefield, Ann Casement herself (a Jungian analyst), and eight members of the International Psychoanalytic Association (IPA) - R.D. Hinshelwood, Jorge Ahumada, Pearl King, Mark Solms, Morris Eagle, Michael Pokorny, Peter Fonagy and Mary Target.
