Human Longings and Masculine Terrors: Masculinity and Separation from Mother

Christina Wieland

Christina Wieland

50 Fernleigh Road, London N21 3AL. [email: chwiel@hotmail.com]

Christina Wieland  

The paper explores two literary texts - Dostoevsky's novel Crime and Punishment and Euripides' play Bacchae - from the point of view of immature masculinity and the catastrophe that can follow if the boy fails to achieve a genuine separation from the maternal object. The author examines the masculine anxieties and defences that arise when the boy fails to work through the Oedipus complex and instead retreats to a dyadic relation with mother which excludes the father. This retreat involves a denial of reality and the creation of a paranoid world in which his own wishes to take possession of mother can be experienced by him as an intrusion by the mother into his own masculine identity and ultimately as castration by the mother. Attempts to resolve this threat to masculinity include the use of anal defences and tyrannical states of mind in the creation of a pseudo-masculinity.

The Inherent Shame of Sexuality

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon

Stevenage, Herts SG1 4AB. [email: mollon@clara.net]

Phil Mollon  

Despite a seemingly sexually liberated culture, sexuality is still disturbing. Freud's original emphasis on the importance of sexuality has largely been lost in much contemporary psychoanalysis, displaced by a focus on attachment. His intuition that sexuality and civilization are in some sense in conflict may have profound implications, throwing light on the nature and function of our linguistic culture and the fetishistic nature of human sexuality. Sexuality is the paradigmatic object of shame and repression, tending to incorporate all else that is repressed. Human beings may tend to long for experience that is unmediated by the linguistic - and this is the promise and the terror of sexuality.

Relatively little has been written about the experience of gift-giving in psychotherapy and what literature there is tends to emphasize more unconscious and destructive motivations. About Supervision: An Interview with Donald Meltzer

Robert Oelsner and Mirta Oelsner

Mirta Oelsner

4119 Dayton Avenue, N Seattle, WA 98103. [email: robertoelsner@aol.com]

[email: mirtaboelsner@aol.com]

Mirta Oelsner  

This interview took place in February 1999 during a supervision weekend held at Donald Meltzer's house at Simsbury near Oxford.1

MBO: Do you think that supervision is a super vision, or a very special vision of the patient?

DM: Well, as you know, in the earlier days of psychoanalysis the supervision was called ‘control’, which was a terrible term - for the supervisor to be controlling the analyst; even at the beginning students didn't like being controlled. It is super in the sense that the supervisor is supposed to have more experience than either the junior or the student; in the supervision almost all the supervisor has to offer is really the proof of his experience, because we are not operating a science in the sense of anything that can be mathematized or quantified. We are working with the quality of things, particularly the quality of emotion and, of course, we all have experiences of life. In many ways, because of their experiences of life, older people are expected to be wiser than young people - which they generally are. Older analysts certainly have had experience of many more clinical situations and therefore are expected to have, and do have, richer powers of discriminating between one analytic situation and another; and this they contribute, or should contribute. It is very much in the spirit of psychoanalysis that this is meant to be a feeding situation - and not force-feeding, but a feeding situation in which what you have to offer is laid before the student or the supervisee for him to select what suits him. I think it must be left really to the richness and the power of your ideas about the clinical material to make it palatable to the person who is being supervised, and you must try to avoid any kind of imposition of your ideas.

Reparation Terminable and Interminable

Jane Polden

Jane Polden

16 Catton Grove Road, Norwich NR3 3NH. email: jane.polden@ntlworld.com

Jane Polden  

Reparation, in psychoanalytic and particularly Kleinian thinking, is often seen as central to the establishment of a creative capacity for love and concern. But apparent reparative urges may have obsessional and narcissistic aspects which militate against the capacity to use an object and thus against the emergence of genitality and true creativity. In particular, ‘reparative’ strivings may be a defence against feared parental envy and against the agonies and anxieties inherent in the act of asserting a separated self. The obsessional need to repair is considered in developmental and clinical terms and in relation to the practice and culture of psychoanalysis.

The Three Vertices: Science, Art and Religion

Meg Williams

Meg Williams

Surrey GU10 5RF. [email: meghwilliams@yahoo.co.uk website: www.artlit.info]

Meg Williams  

Bion saw science, art and religion as vertices of knowledge or ‘devotion to the truth’ that were equally important to psychoanalysis and that needed to be brought into fruitful communication. This paper considers their complementary qualities, in the context of the later thinking of Bion and of some recent lectures by Meltzer on Bion's theory of thinking, which include his second thoughts about the Grid. In particular I want to pay some attention to the ‘neglected’ religious vertex (as Bion saw it), and to the function of cruelty in it, something which Meltzer has suggested arises inherently from the countertransference situation in the context of symbol-formation.1

The Relevance of Evolutionary Psychology for Psychotherapy

Anthony Ryle

Anthony Ryle

London SE1 3SS. [email: Rylecat@aol.com]

Anthony Ryle  

The claims made for the contribution of Evolutionary Psychology to psychotherapy are questioned. The relevance of human evolutionary history is not disputed, but it is argued that insufficient account is taken of the unique features of human beings, that the polemical attacks made on the social and human sciences are irrational, that the hypothetical reconstructions of human evolution are frequently arbitrary and biased, and that the extent to which evolved innate ‘mentalities’ are said to determine social roles ignores the evidence for the plasticity of human brains and for social influences in individual development. In its consistent bias in favour of innate rather than learned and culturally formed processes and in its language and assumptions EP underestimates the inherited and acquired capacities of human societies and individuals to change. It fails to take adequate account of the key evolutionary development whereby humans became symbol-making and symbol-using social animals whose individual psychological development involves processes, the understanding of which requires a new theoretical perspective. These features, combined with the absence of a clear model of practice, seriously limit the contribution of EP to psychotherapy.

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

London

Jean Arundale  

For many years Betty Joseph has led a case discussion group made up of younger psychoanalysts that has created waves of influence in relation to her ideas of micro-analysis of process together with her development of Melanie Klein's notion of the ‘total transference situation’. The Workshop is based on the assumption that most of the analyst's countertransference is unconscious causing him to be pulled into enactments with the patient, entanglements that are devilishly difficult to step back from and understand, requiring a ‘third’ to be involved. The Workshop provides just this needed third position of felt observation, and over the years the participants have learned to trust each other and to become familiar with each other's strengths, weaknesses and idiosyncrasies as they decipher the unconscious relationships going on in their consulting rooms. The papers of this book represent a culmination of the techniques and insights that have evolved since the Workshop's beginning in 1962.

Joseph's enquiry, in particular, has been into those patients whose genuine emotional states are, in the words of one of her seminal papers, ‘difficult to reach’, patients who are more often encountered in clinical practice than one might expect. These are patients whose analyses either appear to be moving along in a co-operative, unconflicted way but without real change, or else present as more overtly stuck and inaccessible to analytic improvement, patients who fear being emotionally unsettled or knocked off balance by contact with a turbulent unconscious, so that they convert the analysis into a haven for maintaining their psychic equilibrium. Joseph emphasizes the antidote: immediate, alive, present emotional experience in the session through the re-owning of projective identifications. These patients ‘act on us to feel things’, the vehicle of projection, to pull us into their defensive systems or into acting out desired relationships, forestalling psychic change.

The book begins with an admirable introduction by the editors, Edith Hargreaves and Arturo Varchevker, emphasizing the spirit of enquiry and the struggle to understand that imbues the workshop. The eleven chapters are difficult to do justice to in the format of a review, as each has its own personal perspective and deserves attention in its own right. After each paper there are commentaries by other members of the workshop that give a sense of what the seminar discussions are like, allowing the reader, with a bit of a nudge to the imagination, a feeling of participation and an urge to join in, whether agreeing or disagreeing with the points at hand.

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner

Bath

Fiona Gardner  

Although published a few years ago this book has been rightly brought to the attention of the British Journal of Psychotherapy. It offers an essential guide to those in training, to the less experienced and to all those of us who from time to time need help in thinking through how to deepen our work.

Jane Hall draws on her long experience as a social worker, as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist and as a psychoanalyst to present an easily accessible exploration of how to move from superficial concerns and the push to give advice to the underlying unconscious conflict and dynamics of the work. She writes that the book is meant to help ‘the beginning psychoanalyst who recognizes that analysis is the treatment of choice but is confronted by a patient who only wants counselling’ (p. 2). Her central argument is that ‘people often need to wade rather than dive directly into deep water’ (p. 3), and so her book gently and thoughtfully takes us through the processes that enable patients to chose to deepen their treatment as they come to understand and appreciate how it works. This is a serious and respectful approach to the needs and autonomy of the patient, and Hall maintains that the psychotherapist who withstands the patient's pulls and pushes away from exploring the inner life and who maintains the conviction that analytic work is effective in the face of the patient's despair and negativity gains the patient's trust and deepens the work.

Each chapter offers clear useful insights illustrated by clinical examples that demonstrate the range of Hall's experience as clinician, teacher and supervisor. The first chapter sets the stage and explores the ongoing structure of the treatment. A central thesis is the notion of benevolent curiosity - a phrase learned by Hall from her reading of Ella Sharpe's collected papers (indeed the influence of Ella Sharpe is present throughout the book). It is clearly easier to practise benevolent curiosity with some patients rather than others but she holds this as the most important attitude to strive for and to maintain during the work.

Gertrud Mander

Gertrud Mander

London

Gertrud Mander  

This book has been hailed as the first comprehensive Jungian approach to supervision to be published, exploring key aspects of the supervisory process and breaking new ground in developing a body of theory on supervision. It has in fact emerged from a series of twelve-week supervision events called Thinking About Supervision developed and organized in the late 1990s by the editors on behalf of the Society of Analytical Psychology. It joins a plethora of recent books on supervision, which indicate a growing interest in supervision as a practice that is taught and theorized about and that has led to textbooks written for trainees and practitioners. Interestingly this book's title almost replicates the title of a book on supervision by the American psychoanalyst Robert Langs, Doing Supervision and Being Supervised (1943), which concentrated on the ‘secure frame’ and is mentioned by one of the contributors. This ‘coincidence’ may indicate that writing about supervision is topical, yet that it is not easy to be original.

Supervision has been practised in the analytic profession since Freud gave Jung advice on his first analytical case in 1909 without calling it supervision, while discovering countertransference in the process. Reading this book makes one realize that there is no such thing as ‘Jungian supervision’ per se, only supervision practised by Jungian analysts who have taken on board ideas and concepts from Freud, Klein, Bion, and even from counsellors and from social workers like Janet Mattinson (1975), who borrowed the term ‘reflection process in supervision’ from the American analyst H.F Searles (1955). This concept is, together with that of ‘learning from experience’, the only theory specifically designed for analytic supervision, though it has since become firmly a part of analytic language.

The claim in the book's subtitle is in fact a question. Is supervision really in search of a theory, is it an activity separate from analysis or rather, as the last chapter ‘Evolving a theory’ indicates, is it simply inseparable from the work and training of analysts, psychotherapists and counsellors, and therefore ‘cannot be considered as an essentially different activity but only a part of it’ (p. 224)? Indeed, it was not always separate in the past, as two of the book's most interesting contributors describe in their historical overview of supervision (Wharton and Martin).

Stephen Frosh , Ann Phoenix and Rob Pattman

Rob Pattman

London WC1E 7HX. [email: s.frosh@bbk.ac.uk]

Rob Pattman  

From the perspective of psychotherapists involved in working with young men, it is particularly interesting to consider ways in which boys may construct versions of their masculinities through an amalgam of social and personal discourses. Amongst the issues relating to young masculinities to arise systematically in research studies and in psychotherapeutic work, two are of particular interest for emerging understanding of the emotional consequences of new structures of masculine identities. These are the relationship boys have with their fathers, and the impact of social discourses on homosexuality. In this paper, material is presented from one boy who participated in an in-depth interview study of boys in London secondary schools. This boy reveals in unusual detail the ways in which dominant discourses on being ‘gay’ and on fathers govern the construction of contemporary young masculinities, even when boys themselves seek to resist these discourses. It is suggested that consideration of the operation of these discourses in young people's lives is a relevant concern for psychotherapists.

Antonia Murphy  

I was glad to be asked to review this book. The request was somewhat serendipitous, given the subject matter, as I had recently ended a long period of work with a violent and potentially suicidal patient. I was also currently helping a supervisee come to terms with the suicide of a patient whom she had assessed as very high risk and had referred on to specialist services. Both these patients presented in general practice (primary care) via their GPs. The treatment of dangerous patients is not solely confined to the settings of forensic psychiatry, hospitals, or secondary and tertiary mental health services. Patients with personality disorders which may indicate varying degrees of ‘danger’ can present in the ordinary course of general practice and in non-statutory and voluntary sector services. Thus I have to admit to some slight disappointment alongside much admiration for this volume because of its emphasis on the treatment of such patients in specialist settings and the implication that psychodynamic therapy is only possible in such contexts. It would have been interesting to have included in the volume an additional chapter from the vantage point of primary care, perhaps written from the multi-disciplinary perspective of this setting. It has been my experience that some very disturbed patients can be contained and treated in primary care teams which are well resourced and have the right degree of therapeutic expertise in the team.

Having said this, however, standing on the shoulders of giants is no bad thing, particularly in this very frightening arena. The experience and expertise which such as Ronald Doctor (formerly psychiatrist at Wormwood Scrubs Prison), John Lowe (psychiatrist in a psychiatric intensive care unit) and Carine Minne (consultant psychiatrist in forensic psychotherapy at Broadmoor) are able to bring to the subject matter of this volume, because of the nature and context of their work, is hugely valuable. What they have to say from their considerable clinical experience speaks to all of us who are, as Bion states, but one of ‘two anxious people together in the room’. Although most jobbing psychotherapists will rarely be working with this degree of pathology either in their private practice or in their work in other settings, there is much on which to draw from the particular understanding of violence which the authors describe in this volume. Each author explores the inherent difficulties of risk assessment and treatment of very violent patients in a sensitive and serious way. The various writers examine the violence described, either threatened or acted out, very carefully, displaying utmost dedication and bringing much needed insight into an area which often provokes fear and, not surprisingly, simplistic and punitive reactions.

The first half of this paper attempts to track and to elaborate Freud's thesis on the mechanism proper to psychosis with particular attention paid to the case of Schreber. It is written emphasizing that Freud was only at the initial stages of his work on the function of the father and that this led to the stumbling blocks he encountered and left him dissatisfied with his work. The second half of the paper looks at the way in which Jacques Lacan took up Freud's work. It looks at how he used it to understand the structure of psychosis in a new way, giving the specific problems that arise in psychosis a central place in the practice of psychoanalysis.

Projection, Introjection and Identity in Anorexia Nervosa

Anthony Winston

Anthony Winston

Warwick CV35 5BW. [email: Anthony.Winston@SWarkPCT.nhs.uk]

Anthony Winston  

In some cases of anorexia nervosa, the mother uses projective identification to produce a state of fusion between herself and her child. This makes it impossible for the child to develop a sense of herself as separate. The rejection of food represents a symbolic rejection of these maternal projections. This defence also prevents the healthy introjection of parental objects which is required to establish a sense of identity. The anorexic is left with a profound sense of inner emptiness and an inability to develop adult relationships. The therapeutic relationship can provide a non-invasive environment in which the patient can begin to develop a sense of self. Case material is used to demonstrate how progress was closely linked to the patient's growing awareness of the therapist as a separate individual.

The biographical information which follows is not about Meltzer's personal history, with which I am not familiar, but his history as a psychoanalyst, which he has told us at various times in a very charming way (which makes this an ‘authorized’ biography). It is composed of a series of anecdotes that we might consider as the myth of the birth of a vocation.

The first story takes us back to when Meltzer was 8 years old. He was travelling with his parents along the Mediterranean coast when, with feelings of admiration, a mixture of fear and awe towards the beauty of the horses and the trees, he suddenly became aware of the beauty of the works of man while observing some sculptures. At that moment, he felt that the highest aspiration would be to breathe life and beauty into stone.

His comment on this experience was that he found it most appropriate that the mind should discover its own beauty only after having discovered the beauty of nature and of the works of man that prove it and praise it.

The second anecdote comes from his adolescence. In an interview in Brazil in 1988, he recounted his first contact with psychoanalysis at the age of 16. This occurred when the brother of his first girlfriend was training in psychoanalysis and gave him a book by Freud to read.

In 1978 (ten years prior to that interview) Meltzer wrote in the introduction to his book, The Kleinian Development, that he had already read Freud for the first time by the age of 16. That time, however, he attributed it to the influence of Nathaniel Apter, a friend of his elder sister.

At that time, in the United States, Meltzer's native country, those who aspired to become psychoanalysts were required first to study medicine and then to specialize in psychiatry. When he was 22 and still a medical student, Meltzer read the texts of Melanie Klein for the first time. These works made a deep impression on him. After training in child psychiatry, he started his psychoanalytic training at the Chicago Institute.

Clinical Material: Lian

The solicitor's letter has taken me by surprise. I have been asked to forward all my records concerning a former patient, Lian. She is making a claim against her former employer for unfair dismissal and her solicitor wants to see my records of her psychotherapy in case they can be used to support her claim.

Lian is a 43-year-old woman who was born in Hong Kong and came to this country ten years ago. Her husband had been suffering from a serious heart condition and they came to the United Kingdom so that he could receive better medical care. However, his condition continued to deteriorate and he died five years ago. They had no children. After her husband's death, Lian became increasingly isolated and she was referred to me because she was feeling anxious and depressed. I started seeing her a year ago, offering her once-weekly sessions at the lower end of my fee scale.

Joan Raphael-Leff

Joan Raphael-Leff

London

Joan Raphael-Leff  

Increasingly, we live with an illusion of control - control over nature, over our reproductive bodies, and over illness, damage and death through medical supremacy. This book punctures that illusion, dealing as it does with what happens when nature takes an unexpected course propelling babies into the world before their time, and it charts in minute detail the high emotional and physical toll of medical efforts to keep them alive.

These are stories of life and death - of babies desperately fighting for survival; of mothers and fathers engaging with their baby on the brink of death - helping him hold on for dear life at all costs, facing the prospect of sudden death or, for some, having to find resources in themselves to relinquish their hold so as to enable the non-viable infant to die. However, as the observer notes, despite its frequency in intensive care units, the death of a baby rips away the ‘thin veneer of rationality’ (p. 129) confronting us with ‘terrifying thoughts’.

The author's meticulous observations take place under extreme conditions for all concerned - when life in the NICU (Neonatal Intensive Care Unit) tests the premature and sick babies' fragile processes of integration with excruciating disruptive interventions. There for days, weeks, sometimes even months, mothers are unable to mother their incubated babies and fathers feel helpless. Staff operate under constant strain, routinely administering painful medical procedures and having to make spur-of-the-moment crucial decisions for tiny babies who deteriorate very rapidly. As described, the atmosphere can be one of high irritability as baby, parents and staff evacuate unbearable feelings. Defences tend to evolve under these traumatizing conditions, involving either denial of the reality of the baby's emotional experience or imposition of an adult construction upon it - to avoid seeing the infant's confused struggle for understanding given his/her immature cognitive apparatus (pp. 47-8). Observing in minute detail the spontaneous behaviour and reactions of some of these many babies, Maggie Cohen utilizes her own understanding as a child psychotherapist, and draws on identification, empathy, imagination and residues of infantile experience to describe emotional life in an incubator consisting of the stuff of our worst nightmares. Exposure to overwhelming stimulation and inexplicable frustration beyond the baby's capacity to understand, control, discharge and assimilate while alone and unheld for weeks on end, without protection of a mediating m/other.
